author: Basil of Caesarea
occasion: Basil preaches to warn his congregation against envy, which he presents as a destructive passion that makes a person an ally of the devil and an enemy of God and neighbor.
argument: Basil argues that envy is the most destructive passion of the soul, consuming the envious person from within while doing little harm to its object. He traces envy from the devil through Cain, Saul, Joseph's brothers, and the Jews who crucified Christ, showing it as the root of murder and opposition to God. He then describes how envious people misrepresent virtues as vices and feed on others' misfortunes. The remedy is to regard worldly goods as instruments for virtue rather than objects of happiness, and to pursue virtue itself, which is within our power. He closes by urging his hearers to obey the Apostle and replace envy with kindness and mutual forgiveness.

outline.move: Basil introduces envy as the devil's companion to God's generosity, and describes how it torments the envious person, who can never confess the disease and only finds relief in another's downfall.

He shows the envious person praising others only after they have lost their goods, and identifies envy as the cause of the devil's war on humanity and of Cain's murder of his brother, then recounts Saul's envy-driven persecution of David.

Basil argues that envy is worse than wild beasts because kindness only enrages the envious, illustrates with Joseph's brothers and the Jews' envy of Christ, and warns that envy attacks those closest to us.

He explains that envy harms the envious person like a rebounding weapon, dismisses the popular belief in the evil eye as old wives' talk but says demons use the envious, and describes how the envious slander every virtue with the name of the opposite vice.

Basil turns to the cure: do not count wealth, reputation, or bodily health as true goods, but see them as instruments for virtue and shared benefit, and do not envy those who teach or are praised in the church.
He urges his hearers to look beyond worldly things, transfer their ambition to virtue, recognize that hypocrisy is a fruit of envy, and obey the Apostle by being kind and forgiving to one another.

cast.name: Basil of Caesarea
cast.who: The preacher and author of the homily.

cast.name: Cain
cast.who: The first murderer, presented as the devil's first disciple, who killed his brother out of envy.

cast.name: Saul
cast.who: King of Israel, who persecuted David out of envy despite David's benefits to him.

cast.name: David
cast.who: Saul's benefactor and the object of his envy, later king of Israel.

cast.name: Goliath
cast.who: The Philistine champion whose defeat by David removed Saul's shame; the women's victory song comparing David and Saul then provoked Saul's envy.

cast.name: Joseph
cast.who: Son of Jacob, sold into slavery by his envious brothers, later ruler in Egypt.

cast.name: Pharaoh
cast.who: King of Egypt, whose servants Joseph came to know in prison.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: The Apostle, quoted on envy and murder and on mutual kindness.

cast.name: Solomon
cast.who: Cited as the author of the proverb that a man's envy comes from his companion.

voices.speaker: Paul (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by 'εἰπών' (saying) and by 'πεισθῶμεν τῷ Ἀποστόλῳ' (let us obey the Apostle)

voices.speaker: Solomon (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by 'κατὰ τὸν Σολομῶντος λόγον' (according to Solomon's word)

voices.speaker: The envious person (imagined confession)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by 'ὅτι' after 'ἐρυθριᾷ δημοσιεῦσαι τὴν συμφοράν' (he blushes to make public his misfortune)

voices.speaker: The women singing victory songs (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Embedded in narrative as the words the dancing women attributed to David and Saul, introduced by 'τὸ δεκαπλάσιον... ἀνέθεσαν αἱ χορεύουσαι' (the dancing women attributed tenfold...)

key_terms.sense: Envy, the central passion Basil attacks: grief at a neighbor's prosperity.
The same passion as envy, often with the connotation of the evil eye or malicious bewitching.
The envious person, one who resents and wishes harm on another's good.
The devil, presented as the origin and teacher of envy.
Virtue or excellence, the true good Basil urges his hearers to pursue instead of envying worldly goods.
A neighbor's prosperity or success, the immediate occasion of envy.
Fighting against God, what envy ultimately amounts to.
Hypocrisy, the double-faced behavior that Basil says is a fruit of envy.
Vainglorious or conceited people, from Paul's warning against provoking and envying one another.
Demons, the hateful spirits Basil says use the envious person's eyes and choices for their own purposes.

scripture: Basil quotes the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) and the New Testament. He cites Paul's phrase 'full of envy, murder' (Romans 1:29) and 'Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another' (Galatians 5:26), and Solomon's proverb 'a man's envy comes from his companion' (Proverbs 14:30 LXX). In a modern translation, cite as Romans 1:29, Galatians 5:26, and Proverbs 14:30, noting LXX where the wording differs.
uncertain: The exact date of the homily is not stated in the text.
The precise occasion or liturgical setting is not specified in the text.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Goliath: 'The Philistine champion whose defeat by David removed Saul's shame; the women's victory song comparing David and Saul then provoked Saul's envy.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: καὶ τῆς ἐπὶ τῷ Γολιὰθ αἰσχύνης ἀπαλλαγεὶς, ὅμως ἐπειδὴ ἐν τοῖς ἐπινικίοις τὸ δεκαπλάσιον τῆς τῶν συμβάντων αἰτίας τῷ Δαβὶδ ἀνέθεσαν αἱ χορεύουσαι· Ἐπάταξε Δαβὶδ ἐν μυριάσι, καὶ Σαοὺλ ἐν χιλιάσιν αὐτοῦ
_unresolved_facts.fix: Goliath is mentioned only as 'τῆς ἐπὶ τῷ Γολιὰθ αἰσχύνης' (the shame regarding Goliath) from which Saul was delivered; the text does not say David defeated Goliath, only that Saul was freed from the shame concerning Goliath. The women's song is introduced as 'Ἐπάταξε Δαβὶδ ἐν μυριάσι, καὶ Σαοὺλ ἐν χιλιάσιν αὐτοῦ' — 'Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands' (1 Samuel 18:7 LXX), not a comparison 'of David and Saul' in the sense of ranking them, but a song attributing greater military success to David.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The women singing victory songs (quoted): 'Embedded in narrative as the words the dancing women attributed to David and Saul, introduced by 'τὸ δεκαπλάσιον... ἀνέθεσαν αἱ χορεύουσαι' (the dancing women attributed tenfold...)'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἐπειδὴ ἐν τοῖς ἐπινικίοις τὸ δεκαπλάσιον τῆς τῶν συμβάντων αἰτίας τῷ Δαβὶδ ἀνέθεσαν αἱ χορεύουσαι· Ἐπάταξε Δαβὶδ ἐν μυριάσι, καὶ Σαοὺλ ἐν χιλιάσιν αὐτοῦ
_unresolved_facts.fix: The women's song is introduced by 'ἐν τοῖς ἐπινικίοις... ἀνέθεσαν αἱ χορεύουσαι' (in the victory celebrations... the dancing women attributed), not by 'τὸ δεκαπλάσιον... ἀνέθεσαν αἱ χορεύουσαι'. The phrase 'τὸ δεκαπλάσιον τῆς τῶν συμβάντων αἰτίας' is Basil's interpretive gloss ('tenfold the cause of what had happened'), not the women's actual words. The actual quotation is 'Ἐπάταξε Δαβὶδ ἐν μυριάσι, καὶ Σαοὺλ ἐν χιλιάσιν αὐτοῦ' (1 Samuel 18:7 LXX).

_unresolved_facts.claim: Paul (quoted): 'Introduced by 'εἰπών' (saying) and by 'πεισθῶμεν τῷ Ἀποστόλῳ' (let us obey the Apostle)'
_unresolved_facts.fix: Paul is introduced by 'εἰπών' in section 2 for the quote 'Μεστοὺς φθόνου, φόνου' (Romans 1:29), but in section 6 the introduction 'πεισθῶμεν τῷ Ἀποστόλῳ' refers to the Apostle without naming Paul explicitly; the brief should note that 'Paul' is an identification, not explicit in the text at section 6.

The brief should include 'Baskanos' as a significant term: the envious person is imagined confessing 'Βάσκανός εἰμι' (I am an envious/baleful one), and 'βάσκανος'/'βασκανία' is a key designation throughout, not merely a synonym for φθόνος but carrying specific connotations of the evil eye and baleful influence.
